Jvari Monastery

A 6th-century church on a cliff above the meeting of the Aragvi and Mtkvari — the starting point of Georgian architecture.

Time needed
1 h
From Tbilisi
27 km · 0:35
Road
Paved
Car needed
Economy class
Season
All year
Entry
free

Jvari is the building Georgian architecture starts from. It was raised between 586 and 605 on the rocky hill above Mtskheta, on the spot where Saint Nino is said to have set up the first wooden cross in the 4th century. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1994 as part of the Historical Monuments of Mtskheta.

Architecturally it is a turning point. Jvari established the tetraconch plan — four apses around a central domed space, fully symmetrical — and that model was copied across the Caucasus for the next several centuries. The building itself is almost aggressively plain: no frescoes, no gilding, only stone, proportion and a column of light falling from the dome.

The other half of Jvari is the view. From the edge of the rock you look down on:

  • The confluence of the Aragvi and the Mtkvari, where two differently coloured rivers meet without mixing at first
  • Mtskheta laid out like a model, with the dome of Svetitskhoveli at its centre
  • The old royal plain and the first ridges of the Greater Caucasus behind it

Lermontov wrote Mtsyri from this landscape, which makes the hilltop a minor pilgrimage for Russian readers as well as Orthodox ones. The monastery is active, and at night it is floodlit and visible from the town below.

Practical advice

Come early in the morning or towards evening; at midday coach parties arrive in waves and there is no shade at all on the rock. The wind here is strong in every season, and in winter the icy forecourt is genuinely slippery. The dress code is enforced: headscarf and long skirt for women, long trousers for men, with free wraps available at the entrance. An hour is enough. There are toilets by the car park but no café; souvenir stalls open in summer.

How to get there from Tbilisi

Leave Tbilisi northwards on the Georgian Military Highway (E117) and do not turn off into Mtskheta itself — the Jvari access road is a separate turning on the left bank of the river, just after the bridge. From there a narrow but fully asphalted switchback climbs about seven kilometres to the top of the cliff. The whole trip takes a little over half an hour. There is a large free car park at the summit and fuel stations at the Mtskheta turn-off. An economy car is perfectly adequate; in winter the only issue is ice on the bends.
